A British defence startup founded by a former Anduril director, which is building virtual battlefields where AI-powered autonomous weapons practice fighting, has raised $70m in a Series A fuding round, less than six months after its  $30m seed funding round.

Agon's new funding round was led by existing investor Northzone, along with other existing investors, including Lakestar, XYZ, Lux Capital, Global Founders Capital, and Speedinvest.

The UK Sovereign AI Fund, the UK government's VC fund established to scale up UK AI startups, and the National Security Strategic Investment Fund (NSSIF), the UK government's deeptech venture capital fund for national security and defence, have invested together for the first time, Agon said.

Roelof Botha, who led Sequoia between 2022 and 2025, has also invested.

The latest funding round values Agon at $450m and Agon says it marks one of the largest European defence technology Series A rounds of 2026. In total, it has now raised around $100m.

Founded in 2026, Agon is pitching itself as a startup that builds the infrastructure that designs, trains and iterates AI systems faster than adversaries. 
Its tech provides its customers with AI training data to help in combat. The startup is making a play about its sovereign credentials, saying that Europe needs the sovereign capability to train and evolve AI.

It says it has signed initial partnerships with European defence companies and government customers.
Its “synthetic” battlefield is aimed at helping its customers train their weapons to repel enemies, so for instance, using AI technology, counterdrone weapons can practice downing drone swarms or test how autonomous systems operate when communications are disrupted, navigation is degraded or adversary tactics change.

It claims that its technology gives defence companies, AI developers and governments the best chance of success on the battlefield.

UK-founded Agon, which has offices in London and Berlin, was founded by former soldier and former Anduril director Tristam Constant and Junaid Hussain, who is the co-founder of another British defence startup, Cambridge Aerospace and Google-backed AI and gaming company Iconic.

The new funding will be used to build its engineering and research teams, speed up the development of its platform, and expand its work with its clients.

Constant, co-founder and CEO of Agon, said: "Europe is in an AI arms race as
we enter the era of agentic warfare: intelligent agents and machines that will need to
understand their environment, make decisions and adapt at a speed and scale that humans
alone cannot match. 
 

"We exist to build the sovereign infrastructure and AI foundation
models to allow us to train, test, and evolve autonomous defence systems – in Europe, for
Europe – to outperform adversary capabilities.

“Agon was born out of a project to bring together a coalition of European founders,
operators, researchers, veterans, investors, and governments to build what we collectively
believe to be urgently needed for our sovereignty and safety.”
